case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an appellate court must remand to an agency after finding the agency used the wrong legal standard (rather than affirming on alternative grounds), and whether a party challenging agency removal protections must prove case-specific prejudice before a court will reach the merits of the separation-of-powers claim.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Administrative law remand/record-review principles associated with the APA and Chenery doctrine (judicial review of agency action), and Article II of the U.S. Constitution (separation of powers / President’s removal authority) as applied to statutory tenure protections for FDIC Board members and FDIC administrative law judges.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Calcutt argues the Sixth Circuit violated SEC v. Chenery by affirming the FDIC’s enforcement decision even after concluding the FDIC Board applied incorrect legal standards; once the agency’s reasoning is legally flawed, the court must remand to allow the agency to apply the correct standards in the first instance. He also argues the Sixth Circuit wrongly treated Collins v. Yellen as imposing a strict, concrete proof-of-prejudice prerequisite that effectively blocks courts from adjudicating removal-protection challenges on the merits, even where the structure itself allegedly violates Article II.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FDIC contends the Sixth Circuit was entitled to deny remand because the outcome was correct on the existing record under the proper legal standard (i.e., any error was harmless and remand would be pointless). On the constitutional issue, the FDIC argues the Sixth Circuit correctly rejected Calcutt’s removal-protection challenge because, under Collins, a challenger must show the allegedly unconstitutional tenure protections actually caused harm in his case (a remedial/prejudice showing), and Calcutt failed to do so.
key_precedents: Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (2010)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error/“idle and useless formality” point (Wyman-Gordon; Morgan Stanley) is the strongest case for affirmance, but it presupposes we can say the sanction is legally inevitable on this record. Where the FDIC applied the wrong governing standard in a discretionary sanctions determination, declaring inevitability would require the court of appeals to perform the agency’s evaluative weighing under the correct test, which Chenery forbids and which Justice Kavanaugh’s Ventura/Gonzales v. Thomas “ordinary remand rule” squarely counsels against. Those harmless-error precedents are better read as narrow exceptions for ministerial or truly foreordained outcomes, not for substituting judicial judgment for agency discretion under a different legal framework. On the Article II issue, I remain aligned with Justice Kagan that Collins is best treated as remedial, so we can decide narrowly on Chenery grounds and remand without reaching constitutional questions.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s reliance on Wyman-Gordon and Morgan Stanley does not justify affirmance here because those cases address situations where remand would be a truly ministerial formality, not where the agency applied the wrong governing legal standard in a discretionary sanctions determination. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize through Chenery and the ordinary remand rule (Ventura; Gonzales v. Thomas), Article III courts may not supply the agency’s missing application of a corrected standard without substituting judicial judgment for executive discretion the statute assigns to the FDIC. Even under a textualist view of the APA, “harmless error” cannot be expanded to let courts declare inevitability when the very point of the corrected test is how the agency weighs facts and exercises discretion. On the Article II question, I remain aligned with Justice Gorsuch that Collins is best treated as remedial; converting it into a merits gatekeeper would improperly insulate structural violations from judicial review and distort separation-of-powers enforcement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Chenery/ordinary-remand point is the strongest: courts must not do the agency’s discretionary work under a corrected standard. But on this record, the court of appeals did not engage in new factfinding or policy balancing so much as recognize that, given the FDIC’s unchallenged findings and the statutory predicates already satisfied, any alternative sanction would be unlawful—making remand an “idle and useless formality” in Wyman-Gordon terms and consistent with Morgan Stanley’s harmless-error approach. Justice Kavanaugh’s Ventura/Gonzales v. Thomas line appropriately polices issues committed to agency discretion in the first instance, yet it is less forceful where the only remaining step is a legally compelled consequence of established findings rather than an open-ended discretionary calibration. On the Article II question, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Kagan’s view (shared by the Chief) that Collins is purely remedial in a way that avoids any gatekeeping function; Collins’ causation requirement is best read to prevent automatic vacatur absent a traceable, case-specific link, and Calcutt has not made that showing here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that remand can be an “idle and useless formality” under Wyman-Gordon and that harmless-error principles (Morgan Stanley) sometimes permit affirmance—does not fit this case because the FDIC applied the wrong legal standard in a discretionary debarment decision where the agency’s weighing and calibration are the very thing Congress assigned to it. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize through Chenery and the ordinary remand rule (Ventura; Gonzales v. Thomas), once the governing framework is corrected, a reviewing court cannot declare the same sanction inevitable without substituting its own evaluative judgment for the agency’s and thereby undermining APA regularity and fairness to the individual whose livelihood is at stake. Alito’s attempt to distinguish Ventura by saying the court of appeals did no factfinding still misses the separation-of-functions problem: applying the correct standard to established findings is often the discretionary step, not a ministerial one. On the Article II issue, I remain aligned with Justice Kagan and the Chief that Collins is best treated as remedial rather than a merits gatekeeper; requiring a case-specific causation showing up front would unduly insulate structural defects from review and impair access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that harmless-error doctrine can spare an “idle and useless formality” (Wyman-Gordon; Morgan Stanley), but those cases fit situations where the agency’s path is legally or factually fixed on the existing rationale, not where the agency used the wrong governing standard in a discretionary sanction decision. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize (Ventura; Gonzales v. Thomas), the ordinary remand rule is especially strict when the agency must apply the correct legal standard in the first instance; otherwise the court of appeals necessarily performs the FDIC’s evaluative weighing under a new test, which Chenery forbids. On Alito’s Collins point, I agree with Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor that Collins is primarily remedial—limiting retrospective relief absent causation—not a threshold merits bar that would effectively insulate structural Article II claims from judicial review. Nothing in Alito’s framing shows this was one of the rare cases where the outcome is truly inevitable without substituting judicial judgment for the agency’s.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error point (Wyman-Gordon; Morgan Stanley) has purchase only where the error is genuinely immaterial to an outcome the agency was legally required to reach; it cannot justify affirmance when the agency applied the wrong governing standard in a discretionary sanctions setting and the court of appeals necessarily supplied its own evaluative judgment. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize via Ventura and Gonzales v. Thomas, the “ordinary remand rule” is rooted in the APA’s record-review design and separation of powers: courts review the agency’s reasons, they do not exercise delegated discretion in the first instance under a corrected test. On the removal issue, I remain aligned with Justice Thomas that Collins is principally remedial; treating it as a merits gatekeeping rule would improperly shield structural Article II defects from adjudication and is unnecessary to resolve this case given the Chenery remand. A narrow Chenery-based remand best respects our limited judicial role while allowing Collins to constrain any retrospective relief if causation is absent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is the Wyman-Gordon/Morgan Stanley “idle and useless formality” harmless-error principle, but I don’t think it fits a case where the agency applied the wrong governing standard in a discretionary sanction/causation determination; calling the outcome “inevitable” would require the court of appeals to do the FDIC’s evaluative weighing under the corrected test, which Chenery and the ordinary remand rule forbid. The Chief Justice’s framing is persuasive: once the legal standard is wrong, Ventura and Gonzales v. Thomas counsel a strict remand precisely to preserve institutional roles and ensure the agency applies the correct standard in the first instance. Wyman-Gordon and Morgan Stanley are best read as narrow exceptions for ministerial or truly foreordained outcomes, not as a license for appellate substitution of judgment in an APA accountability setting. On the Article II issue, I remain aligned with Chief Justice Roberts (and Justice Thomas) that Collins is primarily remedial; treating it as a categorical merits gate would unduly insulate structural claims and is in tension with Free Enterprise Fund’s approach.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Wyman-Gordon and Morgan Stanley recognize harmless-error review to avoid an “idle and useless formality,” but those cases cannot be stretched to permit affirmance where the agency used the wrong governing legal standard in a discretionary sanctions determination. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize (Ventura; Gonzales v. Thomas), the “ordinary remand rule” reflects a structural allocation: once the legal framework changes, it is for the FDIC—not an Article III court—to perform the evaluative weighing in the first instance, and a court cannot deem the outcome inevitable without effectively exercising that delegated discretion, contrary to Chenery. I also agree with Justice Thomas that Collins is best understood as remedial rather than a merits gatekeeping rule; it may constrain retrospective relief absent causation, but it should not be used to insulate structural Article II claims from adjudication. Nothing in Alito’s harmless-error authorities genuinely undermines that textual and precedential boundary between judicial review and agency decisionmaking here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that harmless-error doctrine can avert an “idle and useless formality” (Wyman-Gordon; Morgan Stanley), but that logic is too thin where the agency used the wrong governing standard in a discretionary sanctions determination—because inevitability is not something a court can assert without doing the FDIC’s weighing itself. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize via Chenery and the ordinary remand rule (Ventura; Gonzales v. Thomas), once the court of appeals identified the wrong legal test, the APA’s allocation of decisionmaking requires the agency—not the judiciary—to apply the correct framework in the first instance, especially when practical consequences for an individual’s livelihood are substantial. Wyman-Gordon and Morgan Stanley do not authorize appellate substitution of discretion under a corrected legal standard; they are at most narrow exceptions for truly ministerial outcomes where the agency’s lawful reasoning path is already fixed on the record. On the Article II issue, Justice Kagan’s reading of Collins as primarily remedial remains more consistent with preserving review of structural claims while allowing causation limits to shape the remedy rather than block adjudication altogether.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (1943), a reviewing court may not uphold agency action on a rationale the agency itself did not adopt; once the court of appeals concluded the FDIC Board applied the wrong legal standard, the ordinary course is to state the correct standard and remand for the agency to apply it in the first instance, preserving proper institutional roles and avoiding appellate fact- or discretion-substitution. Harmless-error review does not justify affirmance where the error goes to the governing standard in a discretionary enforcement decision, because the court cannot reliably deem the outcome inevitable without intruding on the agency’s delegated judgment. On the Article II question, Collins v. Yellen addresses remedy and suggests a showing of causation may be required for retrospective relief, but it does not impose a rigid, case-specific prejudice prerequisite that bars courts from reaching the merits of a structural separation-of-powers challenge. A narrow ruling requiring remand under Chenery resolves the case on nonconstitutional grounds and best protects institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the APA, a reviewing court must evaluate “the grounds upon which the agency acted” on the administrative record, 5 U.S.C. § 706, and Chenery forbids affirmance on a rationale the agency itself did not adopt. Once the court of appeals concluded the FDIC applied the wrong legal standard in a discretionary enforcement determination, it exceeded the judicial role by supplying its own application of the correct standard rather than remanding to the agency to decide in the first instance. On the Article II question, Collins concerns remedy, not whether a court may reach the merits of an unconstitutional removal restriction; requiring a case-specific showing of prejudice as a threshold merits bar improperly insulates structural constitutional violations from judicial review. Free Enterprise Fund confirms that multi-layer removal protections raise serious Article II problems and that courts must be able to adjudicate those claims, with any prejudice inquiry properly addressed to the remedy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chenery bars courts from supplying post hoc rationalizations for agency action, but it does not compel a remand when the agency’s legal misstep was irrelevant to the outcome and the record makes clear the agency was bound to reach the same result; in that circumstance, harmless-error principles permit affirmance to avoid an “idle and useless formality.” See SEC v. Chenery Corp., 318 U.S. 80 (1943); NLRB v. Wyman-Gordon Co., 394 U.S. 759, 766 n.6 (1969) (plurality); Morgan Stanley Cap. Grp. Inc. v. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1, 554 U.S. 527, 545 (2008). On the Article II removal issue, Collins v. Yellen indicates that even assuming an unconstitutional removal restriction, a litigant must show case-specific harm traceable to the restriction to obtain relief, and Calcutt has not shown that any President would have removed the relevant FDIC officials and altered his proceeding. Free Enterprise Fund confirms structural limits but does not dispense with Collins’ remedial prejudice requirement for setting aside an agency action in an individual enforcement case.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (1943), a reviewing court may not affirm agency action on a rationale the agency itself did not adopt; when the agency applies the wrong legal standard in a discretionary enforcement decision, the ordinary course is remand so the agency can exercise its judgment under the correct rule rather than the court substituting its own. The FDIC’s harmless-error theory is too thin where the sanction (industry debarment) is discretionary and the record does not compel the same outcome under the proper standard, making remand necessary to protect fairness and regularity in agency adjudication. On the removal-protections question, Collins v. Yellen (2021) addresses remedy and requires a showing of harm for retrospective relief, but it should not be read to impose a rigid, case-specific prejudice prerequisite that prevents courts from reaching the merits of serious Article II structural claims; that approach would unduly insulate potentially unconstitutional structures from review and undermine access to justice. Consistent with Collins and Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010), courts should adjudicate the constitutional claim and then tailor any remedy to any demonstrated prejudice, rather than using lack of prejudice as a gatekeeping merits bar.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (1943), a reviewing court generally may not affirm agency action on a rationale the agency itself did not adopt, especially where the agency applied an incorrect legal standard and the decision entails judgment or discretion that the agency must exercise in the first instance; the APA’s record-review framework does not authorize courts to supply the missing legal analysis as a substitute for remand. While harmless-error principles can sometimes make remand unnecessary, that exception is narrow and does not fit where the court effectively recalibrates the governing standard and then decides the dispositive issue itself rather than allowing the agency to apply the correct standard on the existing record. On the Article II issue, Collins v. Yellen (2021) is best read as a remedial limitation (what relief is available) rather than a strict jurisdictional bar requiring case-specific prejudice before any court may reach the merits of a removal-protection claim; requiring a concrete prejudice showing at the threshold would unduly insulate potentially unconstitutional agency structures from review contrary to Free Enterprise Fund’s separation-of-powers logic. A workable middle ground is to allow merits review of the structural claim while reserving Collins prejudice analysis for the remedy, which preserves both constitutional accountability and administrable remedial rules.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chenery holds that a reviewing court may not affirm agency action on grounds the agency itself did not invoke, and when the agency applied the wrong legal standard in a discretionary adjudication the ordinary course is to remand so the agency can apply the correct rule in the first instance. Allowing a court of appeals to supply its own alternative rationale risks transferring executive discretion to the judiciary in tension with basic separation-of-powers principles reflected in the APA’s record-review model. On the removal issue, Collins v. Yellen speaks to remedy (whether an unconstitutional removal restriction caused compensable harm) rather than imposing a categorical, case-specific prejudice showing as a gatekeeping prerequisite to adjudicating the Article II claim; the structural question may be reached, with any prejudice inquiry reserved for relief. Free Enterprise Fund reinforces that Article II violations in agency structure warrant judicial scrutiny without demanding that every litigant first prove the President would have removed the relevant officer in his particular case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (1943) and the Court’s “ordinary remand rule,” a reviewing court generally may not affirm agency action by supplying its own alternative rationale when the agency applied the wrong legal standard in a decision involving judgment or discretion; Orlando Ventura and Gonzales v. Thomas summarily enforce that principle by requiring remand so the agency can apply the correct standard in the first instance. The APA’s harmless-error principle does not license appellate factfinding or discretionary reweighing that the agency itself never performed under the proper test, especially in penalty/causation determinations where the agency’s reasoning matters for accountability and workability. On the Article II question, Collins v. Yellen treats any case-specific “harm” requirement as going to remedy, not as a categorical merits bar that prevents courts from adjudicating whether tenure protections unlawfully restrict presidential removal. Consistent with Free Enterprise Fund, the Court should reach the merits of the structural claim (while requiring an appropriate showing for retrospective relief), rather than allowing a rigid prejudice screen to insulate potentially unconstitutional agency structures from review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (1943), a reviewing court may not affirm agency action on a rationale the agency itself did not adopt; if the agency applied the wrong legal standard in a way that implicates discretion or evaluative judgment, the proper course is to vacate and remand rather than substitute the court’s own application of the correct standard. The APA’s harmless-error principle does not license courts to perform the agency’s work where the error goes to the legal framework the agency used to reach its decision, because that undermines the statutory allocation of decisionmaking to the agency and Chenery’s demand for reasoned decisionmaking on the agency’s stated grounds. On the removal issue, Collins v. Yellen speaks to remedy, not a threshold bar to adjudicating an Article II structural violation; requiring a concrete, case-specific prejudice showing before even reaching the merits risks insulating potentially unconstitutional tenure protections from judicial review. Free Enterprise Fund confirms that Article II defects in removal restrictions are justiciable structural claims, and Collins indicates any prejudice inquiry pertains to what relief, if any, follows from that violation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the APA’s record-review framework and Chenery, a reviewing court generally may not uphold agency action on a rationale or legal standard the agency itself did not apply; when the agency used the wrong legal standard in a discretionary enforcement adjudication, the “ordinary remand rule” requires sending the matter back for the agency to apply the correct standard in the first instance. SEC v. Chenery Corp. (1943), reinforced by Ventura and Gonzales v. Thomas, reflects a procedural-fairness principle: courts should not substitute their own judgment for an agency’s on questions committed to agency discretion, even if the record might support the result. On the Article II issue, Collins v. Yellen is best read as addressing remedy (whether relief is warranted) rather than imposing a categorical, case-specific prejudice prerequisite to reaching the merits of a structural separation-of-powers challenge, particularly where the challenged insulation affects accountability across the enforcement process. Practical consequences also favor allowing merits review while calibrating relief to any demonstrated harm, rather than using a prejudice showing to foreclose adjudication of potentially unconstitutional agency structures.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an appellate court must remand to the FDIC when it finds the agency applied the wrong legal standards, and whether a party must prove concrete harm to obtain merits review (and relief) on separation-of-powers challenges to FDIC/ALJ removal protections.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Administrative Procedure Act review principles as articulated through SEC v. Chenery (remand requirement when agency relied on incorrect rationale) and Article II of the U.S. Constitution (Executive power and permissible limits on removal of executive officers), with related FDIC enforcement/adjudication provisions governing agency proceedings.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Calcutt argues the Sixth Circuit violated Chenery by affirming (or effectively sustaining the outcome) after concluding the FDIC Board used incorrect legal standards, instead of remanding to let the agency apply the correct standards in the first instance; he also argues the Sixth Circuit misread Collins v. Yellen by requiring a heightened, concrete showing of prejudice/harm before courts will even reach the merits of his Article II challenge to the FDIC Board’s and FDIC ALJs’ tenure/removal protections (including alleged 'double for-cause' insulation), thereby insulating unconstitutional structures from judicial correction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The FDIC argues the Sixth Circuit permissibly declined to remand because any error in the agency’s legal standard did not warrant sending the matter back (i.e., the court could resolve the issue without a remand under ordinary appellate/administrative-law principles); on the constitutional issue, the FDIC contends the Sixth Circuit correctly rejected the removal-protection challenge because Calcutt failed to show that the complained-of removal restrictions actually caused him harm, consistent with Collins’ remedial/harmlessness framework and limits on vacatur or relief absent a showing of prejudice.
key_precedents: SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I), 318 U.S. 80 (1943)
Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, 561 U.S. 477 (2010)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error argument is the principal obstacle, but it depends on treating the agency’s application of the proper standard as a purely mechanical exercise; where the correct rule channels discretionary, evaluative judgment, Chenery II’s warning that a “judicial judgment cannot be made to do service for an administrative judgment” and Ventura/Gonzales v. Thomas require remand. As Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh stress, the Sixth Circuit did not merely disregard a missing explanation—it effectively supplied the agency’s weighing under a different standard, which is precisely the institutional substitution Chenery forbids even if a court believes the result likely. Collins, as Justice Kavanaugh frames it, is best understood as remedial: we can address any Article II defect and calibrate relief without converting causation into an antecedent merits bar that would risk insulating unconstitutional structures from review. A narrow, legitimacy-preserving disposition is to vacate and remand on the ordinary-remand/Chenery ground, leaving any Collins causation showing to be addressed at the remedy stage on remand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error submission rests on the premise that the outcome is “legally compelled,” but that premise itself requires an evaluative application of the correct standard that Chenery II forbids a court to supply in place of the agency—particularly where the standard channels discretion rather than producing a purely mechanical result. Chief Justice Roberts is right to emphasize Ventura and Gonzales v. Thomas: the “ordinary remand rule” applies when the agency must exercise judgment under the proper framework, and § 706’s harmless-error principle cannot be read to authorize appellate reweighing that substitutes judicial judgment for administrative judgment. On the Article II question, I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that Collins is principally remedial, not a merits gatekeeper; treating causation as a threshold bar would effectively insulate unconstitutional removal restrictions from review in tension with Free Enterprise Fund’s approach to structural defects. Nothing in Alito’s account shows this is one of the rare cases where the statute leaves genuinely no discretion such that affirmance would be faithful to the original allocation of authority.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas press Chenery/Ventura as a categorical institutional rule against appellate courts applying a corrected standard in the first instance, but I do not read Chenery II to forbid affirmance where the governing law leaves no real room for a different outcome on this record; harmless-error review in § 706 exists to prevent remands that are purely formal. Burlington Truck Lines and Chenery are at their apex when the agency offers no reasoned basis or when the court is tempted to uphold on a new rationale the agency never adopted; here the court is not inventing a rationale so much as recognizing that, under the correct legal standard, the record compels the same result. On Article II, Justice Kavanaugh is right that Collins is remedial, but its causation requirement still counsels against vacating a completed adjudication absent a concrete link between the removal restriction and the enforcement decision, given the practical costs to lawful regulation. I therefore remain unpersuaded that the “ordinary remand rule” should override harmless-error principles when remand would not change anything the agency could lawfully do.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that harmless-error review can avoid an empty remand when the outcome is truly compelled, but that premise collapses here because the corrected standard channels discretion and evaluative weighing; declaring “inevitable” effectively requires the court to do the agency’s sanction judgment itself. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Chenery and the Ventura/Gonzales v. Thomas ordinary-remand rule are not mere anti-formalism—they protect accountable, first-instance administrative decisionmaking when the agency applied the wrong legal framework. Alito’s reliance on § 706 harmless error cannot overcome Chenery II’s warning that a “judicial judgment cannot be made to do service for an administrative judgment,” especially in high-stakes enforcement actions affecting livelihoods. On the Article II issue, Justice Kavanaugh’s point that Collins is principally remedial reinforces that causation belongs in tailoring relief, not as a threshold bar that would risk insulating unconstitutional removal restrictions from review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that APA harmless-error review can spare a pointless remand when the result is legally compelled—has force in the right kind of case, but it doesn’t fit one where the corrected standard requires evaluative judgment rather than a purely mechanical application. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Ventura/Thomas embody an ordinary remand rule precisely to prevent courts from doing the agency’s discretionary work; calling the outcome “inevitable” here effectively reweighs the merits under a different standard, which Chenery II forbids (“a judicial judgment cannot be made to do service for an administrative judgment”). Alito’s effort to cabin Chenery to post hoc rationalizations doesn’t answer that problem, because the Sixth Circuit’s affirmance depends on supplying the missing administrative application of the correct standard, not merely ignoring a harmless misstep. On the Article II point, I remain persuaded by Roberts and Sotomayor that Collins is remedial: causation can limit relief without becoming a threshold bar that would insulate potentially unconstitutional tenure protections from merits review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error argument has force only where the governing law makes the result mechanically compelled, but here the corrected standard channels the FDIC’s evaluative discretion; under Chenery II, a court’s assurance of “inevitability” risks making a judicial judgment do service for an administrative one. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Ventura/Gonzales v. Thomas reinforces that institutional allocation: when the agency applied the wrong legal rule, the ordinary course is remand for the agency to exercise its delegated judgment in the first instance, not appellate reweighing disguised as harmless error. Alito is right that Burlington Truck Lines/Chenery target post hoc rationalizations, yet their premise is broader—review must rest on the agency’s actual reasoning under the correct standard, and § 706 harmless-error cannot be stretched to authorize a substitution of decisionmaker. On Article II, I remain persuaded by Justice Kavanaugh that Collins is remedial; requiring case-specific causation as a threshold bar would effectively insulate unconstitutional tenure protections from merits review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error argument has force only if the corrected standard leaves no room for agency evaluative judgment; but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, this is the Chenery/Ventura/Thomas paradigm where the governing standard channels discretion and weighing, so a court of appeals cannot declare the outcome “inevitable” without effectively supplying the agency’s judgment. Burlington Truck Lines reinforces that point: judicial review cannot be sustained by substituting a different rationale or application than the agency actually made, even if the court believes the record points strongly one way. On Article II, I remain persuaded by Roberts (and Kagan) that Collins is remedial—causation/prejudice can limit retrospective relief on remand, but it should not be converted into a threshold bar that insulates structural defects from merits review. Given those institutional and precedent-based constraints, vacatur and remand is the narrow, legitimacy-protecting course.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that APA harmless-error review can make remand a needless formality where the result is “legally compelled,” but that characterization collapses Chenery’s core constraint into a prejudice inquiry and invites judicial substitution in a domain Congress assigned to the agency. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize via Ventura and Gonzales v. Thomas, when the agency applied the wrong legal standard in a discretionary, evaluative determination, a court cannot declare the outcome “inevitable” without itself doing the relevant weighing—something Chenery II forbids because “a judicial judgment cannot be made to do service for an administrative judgment.” I also agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh that Collins is principally remedial; it does not justify converting case-specific causation into a threshold bar to reaching the merits of a structural Article II claim, especially where that would tend to insulate potentially unconstitutional tenure protections from review. Nothing in Alito’s reliance on § 706 harmless error overcomes the text-and-structure-based allocation of decisionmaking authority reflected in Chenery/Ventura, so vacatur and remand remain the institutionally correct course.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s harmless-error argument presses the practical concern that remand can be an empty formality, but it depends on a court’s own application of a corrected legal standard in a discretionary sanctions regime—exactly the substitution Chenery and Burlington Truck Lines warn against. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Ventura/Thomas embody an ordinary-remand rule for situations where the legal standard channels evaluative judgment; declaring the result “inevitable” on this record risks judicial reweighing rather than harmless-error policing. I also agree with Justice Sotomayor that procedural fairness matters here: when the agency used the wrong standard, accountability requires the agency—not the court—to decide in the first instance how that standard affects the severity of sanctions. On the Article II issue, I remain persuaded (with Roberts/Kavanaugh) that Collins is principally remedial, so any causation showing goes to the scope of relief, not to foreclosing merits review or excusing the Chenery problem.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Chenery I, a reviewing court may not affirm agency action on a rationale the agency itself did not adopt, and where the agency applied an incorrect legal standard in an area involving judgment or discretion, the “ordinary remand rule” requires sending the matter back for the agency to apply the correct standard in the first instance. This Court has enforced that principle repeatedly, including in Orlando Ventura and Gonzales v. Thomas, rejecting appellate factfinding or application of newly announced standards as a substitute for remand. While the APA’s harmless-error principle can bar relief where an error could not have affected the outcome, it does not permit a court to cure an agency’s legal-standard error by supplying its own discretionary application of the correct standard. On the Article II issue, Collins v. Yellen addresses remedy and requires a showing of causation for retrospective relief, but it does not justify declining to reach the merits of a separation-of-powers claim where the challenged structure plausibly infected the proceeding; at minimum, the lower court should not impose a heightened prejudice threshold that effectively insulates structural defects from review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Chenery, a reviewing court may not affirm an agency action on a ground the agency itself did not adopt; when the agency applied an incorrect legal standard in a discretionary adjudication, the “ordinary remand rule” requires sending the matter back to the agency to apply the correct standard in the first instance. See SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I), 318 U.S. 80, 87–88 (1943); cf. Gonzales v. Thomas, 547 U.S. 183, 186–87 (2006) (per curiam). On the Article II issue, Collins v. Yellen addresses remedy, not whether courts may reach the merits of a structural separation-of-powers claim; requiring a heightened, concrete showing of prejudice to obtain merits review would effectively insulate unconstitutional tenure protections from judicial correction and is in tension with this Court’s treatment of unconstitutional removal restrictions in Free Enterprise Fund. The Constitution’s Vesting of the executive power in the President does not permit courts to evade adjudicating an asserted structural defect by demanding proof of case-specific causation before considering the claim’s validity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chenery establishes that courts may not uphold agency action on grounds the agency itself did not adopt, but it does not require a remand where the agency’s error is immaterial and the outcome is inevitable on the existing record—ordinary harmless-error principles under the APA permit affirmance when no prejudice results. Here, once the court of appeals concluded the correct legal standard was satisfied as a matter of law, a remand would be a pointless formality that would delay finality and undermine practical enforcement interests. On the Article II claim, Collins v. Yellen makes clear that even if a removal restriction is unconstitutional, a party is not entitled to relief absent a showing that the restriction actually caused harm; requiring a concrete showing of prejudice avoids unwarranted vacatur of otherwise lawful enforcement outcomes. Free Enterprise Fund does not compel a different result because the remedy for a structural defect is tailored and does not automatically invalidate completed agency adjudications without a demonstrated nexus to the challenged removal protections.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I), when a reviewing court concludes an agency applied the wrong legal standard in a decision that entails judgment or discretion, the proper course is to remand so the agency—not the court—may apply the correct rule in the first instance; affirming by substituting the court’s own application risks insulating potentially unfair outcomes from the agency’s accountable decisionmaking. That remand principle also advances basic fairness for individuals facing severe professional sanctions, where the choice of standard can materially affect how the record is weighed. On the Article II question, Collins v. Yellen speaks primarily to remedy, not to foreclosing merits review absent a heightened, concrete showing of prejudice; where tenure protections plausibly insulate decisionmakers (including ALJs) in an enforcement proceeding, courts should reach the structural claim and not erect a barrier that effectively denies meaningful judicial review. Consistent with Free Enterprise Fund, the Court should ensure unconstitutional insulation is not left in place merely because a litigant cannot prove, ex ante, exactly how the President would have exercised removal authority in his particular case.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Chenery I, a reviewing court must judge agency action on the grounds the agency actually invoked, and when the agency applied an incorrect legal standard in a discretionary adjudication the ordinary course is remand so the agency can apply the correct standard in the first instance, rather than the court supplying its own merits analysis. Chenery II reinforces that a “judicial judgment cannot be made to do service for an administrative judgment,” and the APA’s harmless-error principle does not authorize an appellate court to cure a foundational legal-standard error by reweighing or refinding what the agency should have decided. On the Article II issue, Collins speaks primarily to remedy: it does not justify withholding merits review of a colorable separation-of-powers claim unless the challenger proves concrete prejudice at the threshold; instead, courts can decide the constitutional question and then tailor relief to any showing (or absence) of harm. A workable, coherent approach is to remand on the Chenery problem and, if a removal restriction is unconstitutional, address remedy under Collins without converting harm into a merits gatekeeping requirement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chenery forbids courts from sustaining agency action on rationales the agency itself did not adopt; when the FDIC applied the wrong legal standard in a discretionary enforcement/adjudicative decision, the proper course is to vacate and remand so the agency may apply the correct standard in the first instance. See SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I), 318 U.S. 80, 87 (1943); Burlington Truck Lines, 371 U.S. 156, 168–69 (1962). On the Article II question, separation-of-powers violations are structural, and Collins v. Yellen addresses remedy, not a heightened prerequisite to merits review; a litigant need not prove concrete prejudice just to obtain a ruling on whether FDIC Board/ALJ removal protections unlawfully insulate executive officers, especially given this Court’s skepticism of “double for-cause” insulation in Free Enterprise Fund. Consistent with Article II’s vesting of executive power and the APA’s limits on judicial substitution for agency judgment, the Sixth Circuit should have reached the merits and, upon finding legal error, provided at least vacatur and remand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I) and Chenery II, when an agency decision rests on an incorrect legal standard and the matter involves judgment or discretion committed to the agency, the reviewing court ordinarily must remand because a “judicial judgment cannot be made to do service for an administrative judgment.” This Court has repeatedly enforced that ordinary remand requirement in similar settings (e.g., Gonzales v. Thomas and INS v. Ventura), and the Sixth Circuit’s approach—finding legal error but then effectively affirming by applying what it believed to be the correct standard itself—cuts against those settled principles and the APA’s basic allocation of decisionmaking. On the Article II question, Collins v. Yellen indicates that a party may need to show causation to obtain retrospective relief, but it does not justify withholding merits review of a properly raised separation-of-powers challenge by imposing an extra threshold of concrete prejudice where the claim is directed at an ongoing structural defect (cf. Free Enterprise Fund). The prudent, institutionally modest course is to adhere to Chenery’s workability and restraint: vacate and remand for the FDIC to apply the correct standards in the first instance, while treating remedy for any removal-protection violation under Collins’ remedial/harmlessness framework rather than as a merits bar.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I), 318 U.S. 80 (1943), a reviewing court generally may not affirm an agency’s discretionary decision on a rationale the agency itself did not adopt; if the FDIC applied an incorrect legal standard and the correct application entails judgment committed to the agency, the proper course is remand for the agency to apply the right standard in the first instance. While the APA permits harmless-error review, 5 U.S.C. § 706, that doctrine cannot be used to substitute the court’s factfinding or discretionary weighing for the agency’s, particularly where the legal standard affects the agency’s evaluative determination. On the Article II question, Collins v. Yellen, 141 S. Ct. 1761 (2021), speaks primarily to remedial entitlement (what relief follows) rather than imposing a categorical bar to reaching the merits absent a heightened showing; requiring concrete prejudice as a threshold to merits review risks insulating potentially unconstitutional removal protections, contrary to the separation-of-powers concerns recognized in Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I), an agency order generally cannot be upheld on grounds the agency itself did not adopt, and when the agency applied an incorrect legal standard in a discretionary enforcement/adjudicatory decision, the ordinary and procedurally fair course is to remand so the FDIC can apply the correct standard in the first instance rather than having the appellate court supply its own merits determination. The APA’s review framework contemplates reasoned agency decisionmaking and meaningful judicial review of the agency’s stated rationale; bypassing remand risks substituting judicial judgment for agency discretion and undermining regular process in high-stakes sanctions cases. On the Article II issue, Collins v. Yellen addresses remedy and harmlessness, but it should not be read to bar merits review of a structural separation-of-powers challenge absent a heightened, case-specific showing of prejudice; the question of relief can be tailored to demonstrated harm without insulating potentially unconstitutional “double for-cause” removal regimes from review (cf. Free Enterprise Fund). Given the practical consequences for fairness in agency adjudication and accountability, I would reverse and require remand, and clarify that merits review is available even if relief may depend on a showing of harm under Collins.
